"Why can't I go into the kitchen, Mummy?" Ira, fourteen, stood in the doorway, cheeks hot. "Dadi just shooed me out like I'm dirty."
Sarika put down the ladle. "You're not dirty, beti. A period is your body working the way it should."
"Then why the rule?"
"It's how Dadi was raised, and it matters to her. In her kitchen we'll respect it for now. But it doesn't mean anything is wrong with you."
"I've got cramps. And I'm starving."
"Then you sit on the sofa with the hot water bottle, and I'll bring your food." Sarika lowered her voice. "Tonight I'll show you the book I bought, the one that explains everything properly. Ask me anything."
Ira sniffed. "Can I ask Dadi why, too?"
"Gently. She might tell you stories from when she was a girl."

qa.q: What did Sarika promise to show Ira tonight?
qa.a: The book she bought, the one that explains everything properly.

qa.q: How did Ira feel when Dadi shooed her out?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and hurt, as if she were dirty.

qa.q: How did Sarika balance Dadi's custom and Ira's needs?
qa.a: She respected the kitchen rule for now but told Ira she is not dirty, and gave her comfort, food and proper information.

qa.q: Why might Dadi hold on to the kitchen rule?
qa.a: It is how she was raised and it matters to her, which is not the same as wanting to shame Ira.

grounding: Shows a girl hurt by a family custom around her period, and a parent respecting the custom while giving her comfort, information and dignity.

passage:
When my first period came at thirteen, I was told to wrap the pads in newspaper, not to touch the pickle jars and not to go near the prayer shelf. Nobody explained anything. I thought I had turned into something shameful overnight. I stopped visiting friends and cried in the bathroom with cramps rather than "make a fuss". Then Uma Masi came to stay. She didn't argue with anyone about the customs. She just said, "Beti, in this house we follow Nani's ways. But your body isn't dirty, and you deserve comfort." She bought me proper supplies and a warm pack, drew diagrams on the back of an envelope and let me ask every embarrassing question. I still keep some of the customs, out of love for Nani. But I don't feel ashamed anymore.
Damini

qa.q: How was Damini told to keep the pads?
qa.a: Wrapped in newspaper.

qa.q: How did Damini feel after being told to hide everything?
qa.a: Damini felt ashamed, as if something shameful had happened overnight, and hid the cramps too.

qa.q: What did Uma Masi do that respected both the family and Damini?
qa.a: She followed Nani's ways without arguing, but made sure Damini had supplies, a warm pack, clear information and room to ask anything.

qa.q: How does Uma Masi seem to see the situation?
qa.a: She sees customs that matter to the family, and also a young person left in shame without information, and she quietly fixes the second.

grounding: Illustrates a girl taught to hide her period and avoid certain spaces feeling shame, and an adult respecting custom while restoring comfort, information and dignity.

passage: At the district hockey academy hostel, the rule wasn't written anywhere, but everyone knew it: girls on their period didn't go into the kitchen, because the old cook, Bhagwati Amma, believed it wasn't proper. Elizabeth, fourteen, got her period during camp week. She skipped the evening snack rather than ask, hid her pads inside a sock, and walked around with her shoulders up, as if she had done something wrong. By Wednesday she was trailing in drills, pale and hungry. Coach Hemant noticed and asked the girls' warden to check on her. That evening he spoke to Bhagwati Amma respectfully: from now on the snack would be carried out to the dining hall for everyone, no questions asked. A basket of pads and a hot water bag went into the girls' washroom, and the warden sat with the girls to explain that periods are a normal, healthy process. Elizabeth ate two bananas. That night the sock stayed in her bag.

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth hide her pads?
qa.a: Inside a sock.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel during camp week?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and embarrassed, walking with her shoulders up as if she had done something wrong, and she was hungry.

qa.q: How did the coach respect the custom while protecting Elizabeth?
qa.a: He didn't fight Bhagwati Amma's belief but had the snack brought to the dining hall for everyone, stocked pads and a hot water bag, and had the warden explain that periods are normal.

qa.q: How might Bhagwati Amma see the kitchen rule?
qa.a: To her it is a proper custom she believes in, not meant as cruelty, so being approached respectfully matters.

grounding: Shows a girl made to hide her period and avoid a space learning shame, and adults respecting the custom while ensuring her comfort, information and dignity.

passage:
Dear Sarita Didi,
You said at the health camp that we could write to you with questions, so I'm writing. Please don't show anyone.
My period started three months ago. At home, Dadi says I must never let Abbu or my brothers know, so I wrap the pads in newspaper and hide them under the mattress, and I sit quietly when my stomach hurts because I can't say why. I understand we don't pray on those days; that's our way, and I don't mind that part. But the hiding makes me feel dirty, like I'm carrying a secret crime.
Is it normal for the pain to make me want to cry? Is there anything that helps? And is it wrong to want Ammi to at least talk about it with me?
Ayesha
Class 8

qa.q: Where does Ayesha hide the pads?
qa.a: Wrapped in newspaper, under the mattress.

qa.q: How does the hiding make Ayesha feel?
qa.a: Ayesha feels dirty and ashamed, as if carrying a secret crime, even though periods are normal.

qa.q: Why is writing to Sarita Didi a good step?
qa.a: Ayesha can get comfort and proper information from a trusted adult, keeping the family's ways while not suffering in silence.

qa.q: How might Dadi see her rule about hiding?
qa.a: Dadi may see it as modesty and proper custom, without realising it is teaching Ayesha shame.

grounding: Shows a girl told to hide her period at home feeling shame, respecting her family's faith while seeking comfort, information and dignity.

subtopic: Menstrual cycle effects on mood and coping
passage: Okay, you asked what it was like growing up with the period rules at home. I'm Rajni, from a village near Almora. When my first period came at thirteen, Dadi said I had to stay in the small back room for five days, not touch the water pot, not go into the kitchen or near the prayer corner. Honestly? The back room hurt the most. It was cold, and I felt like I'd been sent away for being dirty. My best friend Simran's family didn't do any of that, and I felt so ashamed around her. What changed things was Mummy. She didn't fight Dadi about the prayer corner; that was Dadi's faith. But she put a proper mattress, a blanket and a lamp in that room, brought me hot water, sat with me every evening, and told me clearly that my body was healthy, not dirty. And she made sure I never missed school. That mattress felt like dignity.

qa.q: What did Mummy put in the back room?
qa.a: A proper mattress, a blanket and a lamp.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel about staying in the back room?
qa.a: Rajni felt sent away and ashamed, as if being dirty, especially around Simran.

qa.q: How did Mummy balance Dadi's faith with Rajni's dignity?
qa.a: She left the prayer-corner custom alone but made the room comfortable, sat with Rajni, explained the body was healthy, and kept Rajni in school.

qa.q: How might Simran have seen Rajni during those days?
qa.a: Simran may not have understood why Rajni was away or withdrawn, since Simran's family didn't follow those rules.

grounding: Shows a girl kept apart during her period learning shame, and a parent respecting the elder's faith while giving comfort, information and dignity.

passage:
Monday: Rukmini's period started, and Paati told her to sit apart on the back verandah and stay out of the kitchen and the puja room. Rukmini ate from a separate plate, cramps twisting her stomach, feeling as if she'd done something dirty. When her brother Akash asked loudly why she was sitting outside, she wanted to disappear.
Wednesday: Amma sat with her on the verandah with a hot-water bottle and a mat. 'Paati's customs come from her own mother,' Amma said. 'We'll respect the puja room. But you'll sleep in your own bed, eat with us, and you have nothing to be ashamed of.' She answered all Rukmini's questions plainly.
Next month: Rukmini told Akash calmly, 'It's my period. It's normal.' He shrugged and passed her the chutney.

qa.q: What did Amma bring to the verandah?
qa.a: A hot-water bottle and a mat.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel on Monday eating from a separate plate?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, as if she had done something dirty, and wanted to disappear when Akash asked loudly.

qa.q: How did Amma balance Paati's customs with Rukmini's dignity?
qa.a: She kept the puja-room custom but made sure Rukmini slept in her own bed, ate with the family, had comfort and got plain answers.

qa.q: How might Akash see periods by the next month?
qa.a: Akash saw it as ordinary once Rukmini explained calmly, simply shrugging and passing the chutney.

grounding: A girl told to hide her period learns shame, and her mother respects family custom while ensuring comfort, information and dignity.
